extracted.intended_audience: members of the public submitting comments to federal rulemaking (NOAA/NMFS)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical tips for drafting and submitting effective, information-rich public comments on federal rulemakings (NOAA/NMFS), aimed at increasing influence on agency decision-making. Covers timing, content, evidence, formatting, and procedural best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and understand the regulatory document you are commenting on
rubrics_metrics.description: Read and understand the regulatory document you are commenting on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt to fully understand each issue; if you have questions or do not understand a part of the regulatory document, you may ask for help from the agency contact listed in the document. Note: agency contacts can answer questions about the document meaning, but official comments must be submitted through the comment form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin well before the deadline / comment periods close at 11:59 eastern
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment periods close at 11:59 eastern time on the date comments are due - begin work well before the deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan ahead so you can prepare a substantive, supported comment rather than rushing to meet the deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly identify the issues you are commenting on with precise citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly identify the issues within the regulatory action on which you are commenting. If you are commenting on a particular word, phrase or sentence, provide the page number, column, and paragraph citation from the Federal Register document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you choose to comment on the comments of others, identify such comments using their comment ID before you respond to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concise but support your claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Be concise but support your claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no minimum or maximum length for an effective comment, but concise, information-rich comments that clearly communicate and support claims are more likely to have impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base your justification on sound reasoning, scientific evidence, and/or how you will be impacted
rubrics_metrics.description: Base your justification on sound reasoning, scientific evidence, and/or how you will be impacted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency reviewers look for sound science and reasoning. When possible, support your comment with substantive data, facts, and/or expert opinions. You may also provide relevant personal experience. By supporting your arguments well you are more likely to influence agency decision making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address trade-offs and opposing views
rubrics_metrics.description: Address trade-offs and opposing views in your comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the pros and cons and trade-offs of your position and explain them. Consider other points of view and respond to them with facts and sound reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: If you disagree with a proposed action, suggest an alternative and analyze it
rubrics_metrics.description: If you disagree with a proposed action, suggest an alternative (including not regulating at all) and include an explanation and/or analysis of how the alternative might meet the same objective or be more effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives grounded in analysis or explanation are more useful to agency decision makers than mere opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify credentials and relevant experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify credentials and experience that may distinguish your comments from others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you are commenting in an area in which you have relevant personal or professional experience (e.g., scientist, attorney, fisherman, businessman), say so to help reviewers assess the weight of your evidence or assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support economic-effect comments with quantitative and qualitative data
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments on the economic effects of rules that include quantitative and qualitative data are especially helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide numbers, analysis, and qualitative explanation where possible to make economic impacts clear and actionable for reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include examples of how the proposed rule would impact you
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider including examples of how the proposed rule would impact you negatively or positively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete examples—personal or business impacts—help translate abstract regulatory text into real-world consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize issues — comment on those you understand and that affect you most
rubrics_metrics.description: If a rule raises many issues, do not feel obligated to comment on every one—select those issues that concern and affect you the most and/or you understand the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focusing on a few well-supported points is better than thinly addressing many issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to agency-requested specific questions and issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies often ask specific questions or raise issues in rulemaking proposals on subjects where they are actively looking for more information; keep these questions and issues in mind while formulating your comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted responses to agency questions are especially useful because the agency is seeking information on those points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive comments are more influential than unsupported opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Although agencies receive and appreciate all comments, constructive comments (either positive or negative) are the most likely to have an influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive means providing reasoned analysis, evidence, alternatives, or specific suggestions rather than simple statements of support or opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: The comment process is not a vote
rubrics_metrics.description: The comment process is not a vote — one well supported comment is often more influential than a thousand form letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies make determinations based on sound reasoning and scientific evidence rather than a majority of votes; focus on quality and substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form letters / mass form submissions carry less weight than individualized, well-supported comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Form letters are frequently used but a single, well-supported comment may carry more weight than a thousand form letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations may encourage form letters, but agencies evaluate the quality of reasoning and evidence, so individualized, evidence-backed comments are generally more influential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a standardized file naming convention for multiple attachments
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are uploading more than one attachment to the comment web form, it is recommended that you use the following file titles: Attachment1_<insert title of document>, Attachment2_<insert title of document>, Attachment3_<insert title of document>.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardized filenames help agency reviewers distinguish submitted attachments and aid in the comment review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a copy of your comment in a separate file
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a copy of your comment in a separate file — this practice helps ensure that you will not lose your comment if you have a problem submitting it using the Regulations.gov web form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having a local backup protects against upload/network failures and helps with resubmission if needed.
